title: Democrats Win US House and Senate
paragraphs: The Democratic Party has won control of both chambers of the US Congress, in a midterm election widely seen as a major setback for President Donald Trump and the Republican Party.

Voters went to the polls on Tuesday, November 3. By the following day, news organizations projected that Democrats had won a majority in the House of Representatives, flipping more than two dozen districts that had been held by Republicans. Some of those districts had been won by Trump by double digits in the 2024 presidential election. NBC News projected that Democrats were on course for their largest House majority in nearly two decades, although dozens of races remained uncalled.

Democrats also secured a majority in the Senate. According to NBC News, they flipped at least seven seats previously held by Republicans, including seats in Texas, Ohio, North Carolina and Kansas. Kansas had not elected a Democratic senator in nearly a century. Meanwhile, Democrats successfully defended their seats in Georgia and Michigan.

Analysts pointed to several factors behind the result, including rising living costs and the war with Iran. Democrats had made affordability a central theme of their campaign, focusing on issues such as health insurance costs and drug prices. Republican Senator Ted Cruz described the outcome as a "Watergate-level repudiation" and said too many Republicans had failed to understand voters' financial difficulties.

Trump, however, said the losses were not a referendum on him and instead blamed the Republican candidates. Before the election, he had warned that he would call himself "Mr. Veto" if Democrats won Congress, suggesting he would block legislation they passed. After the results, though, he said he would "probably" get along with Democrats.

The new Congress will take office in January. Hakeem Jeffries, currently the leader of House Democrats, has launched a bid to become Speaker of the House. With control of both chambers, Democrats will be able to hold hearings, investigate government officials and shape legislation, although any bill they pass can still be vetoed by the president.
Some races were still being counted, so the final number of seats each party holds had not yet been confirmed.
